Looking back, I can't point to the day it changed. That's the scary part.
In first year Abhinav and I both went to the "leadership circle" on Tuesday evenings. Free chai, big talk about purpose. It was good.
Then it was Tuesdays and Thursdays. Then weekends, "for serious members". Then a "contribution" of a thousand rupees for the Level Two teachings, the ones outsiders "weren't ready for". Then: "Keep your distance from people who drain your energy." Abhinav had started asking questions. So I stopped replying to him.
Each step felt tiny. I only saw the whole thing in March, when I tried to write down how I'd spent the week for a time-management task. Twenty-two hours. Four thousand rupees since October. Almost no old friends.
I sat there staring at the page. Then I called Abhinav. He picked up on the first ring and said, "Took you long enough," and I laughed so hard I nearly cried.
Ujjwal

qa.a: Ujjwal counted twenty-two hours.

qa.a: Ujjwal was shocked and shaken, sitting and staring at the page, because each step had felt tiny and the total had been invisible from inside.

qa.q: What turning point helped Ujjwal see the change?
qa.a: Writing down the week for a time-management task showed the hours, the money and the lost friends in one place, which led Ujjwal to call Abhinav.

qa.q: What was it like for Abhinav when Ujjwal stopped replying?
qa.a: Abhinav was cut off for asking questions, yet stayed ready to help, which shows in how quickly he picked up and joked, "Took you long enough".

Counselling note, Student Wellness Centre. Written by Simran, counsellor, 12 November.
Tanvir, second-year engineering, came in on his own today. He spoke quietly and kept checking his phone. He described joining a "self-mastery" group in February: one weekly session at first, then three, then weekend camps. Since August he has paid for "advanced modules", and was told recently that his roommates were "negative influences" and he should not discuss the group with them or his family.
What I observed: he could not say when things had changed. "Every step made sense at the time," he said twice.
We drew a timeline together on paper, month by month. When he saw it, he went very still.
Next steps: with his agreement, I called his mother while he was in the room and she will visit this weekend. I have booked him for Friday. He agreed to skip this weekend's camp and to keep talking to his roommates.

qa.q: When did Tanvir join the self-mastery group?
qa.a: Tanvir joined in February.

qa.q: What does Tanvir's repeated line "Every step made sense at the time" suggest he feels?
qa.a: It suggests Tanvir feels confused and a little ashamed, unable to see how he got so deep because each demand seemed small on its own.

qa.q: Why was drawing the timeline a useful step?
qa.a: Laying out the months on paper let Tanvir see the whole change at once, which the small steps had hidden, so he could decide from outside the group's view.

qa.q: How might Tanvir's roommates have experienced the months he was told they were "negative influences"?
qa.a: They may have felt pushed away without knowing why, and his renewed openness gives them a chance to reconnect.

grounding: A counsellor records a student who, over months, was drawn into more hours, payments, secrecy and distance from others, and helps him see the whole pattern.

That night she scrolled back to January's photos: her and Amandeep laughing on a college bench. She couldn't work out when she had stopped being that person.

Jyoti, you once asked me why I never talk about my college years. Here's why.
At nineteen I joined a "leadership fellowship" in Hyderabad. At first it was one Saturday a month. Then every Saturday. Then Friday nights too, because the "inner circle" studied special texts nobody outside could understand. Then a small monthly "contribution". Then a bigger one. Each step felt like nothing.
By twenty-one I had stopped visiting home. My elder brother, Irfan, kept asking questions, and the fellowship told me doubters were testing my strength. So I stopped answering his calls.
One day Irfan simply turned up at my hostel with a tiffin of Ammi's biryani. He didn't argue. He said, "Farhan, eat first. Then tell me what a normal week looks like for you now." I started listing it. Halfway through, I heard myself. Every hour, every rupee, every friend, gone one small piece at a time.

qa.q: What did Irfan bring to the hostel?
qa.a: A tiffin of Ammi's biryani.

qa.q: How did young Farhan feel while listing a normal week aloud?
qa.a: Young Farhan was startled and shaken, hearing for the first time how every hour, rupee and friend had gone piece by piece.

qa.q: What choice inside the story became the turning point?
qa.a: Irfan turning up with food and asking for a description of a normal week instead of arguing; saying it aloud let Farhan see the whole change.

qa.q: How might Irfan have felt during the months of unanswered calls?
qa.a: Irfan was likely worried and hurt, yet chose patience, coming with food rather than anger.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how a fellowship took more time, money and distance from family step by step until the whole change was hard to see.

The rain had flooded the lane outside the Forum's hall, and Tejas had a statistics exam at nine the next morning. Still, he stayed. Six months ago it had been one Sunday talk. Now it was five evenings, a monthly "seva fee", and tonight a new step: hand over your phone for a "silence week" so the higher teachings could "settle".
His phone buzzed as he held it out. Disha: "Bhaiya, engagement is on the 14th. You ARE coming, na?"
The senior member watching him said gently, "Family noise. You can explain later. They never understand at first."
Tejas thought: it's only a week. It was always only a week, only one more evening, only a small fee. He put the phone in the basket.
Walking home through ankle-deep water, he tried to remember the last time he'd laughed with Disha. He couldn't, and that frightened him more than the exam.

qa.q: What did the Forum ask Tejas to hand over tonight?
qa.a: His phone, for a 'silence week' so the higher teachings could 'settle'.

qa.q: What was Tejas afraid of on the walk home?
qa.a: Tejas felt frightened that he couldn't remember the last time he'd laughed with Disha, a sign of how far the small steps had pulled him.

qa.q: What could Tejas do before the silence week begins?
qa.a: Take the phone back, reply to Disha about the 14th, and talk to someone outside the Forum about how much time and money it now takes.

qa.q: How might Disha feel if her brother went silent before her engagement?
qa.a: Disha would likely feel hurt and anxious, not knowing why Bhaiya had disappeared just before the 14th.

grounding: Shows a student six months into a group that keeps asking for more time, money and distance from family, each step framed as small.

passage: In January, the Awakening Circle in Hyderabad asked Abhinav for one evening a week. It felt like nothing. In March it was three evenings, plus a "contribution" for the advanced course, where the teacher shared "what the world doesn't want you to know". By May, Abhinav had skipped his cousin's wedding for a retreat and stopped mentioning the group at home, because the seniors said families block your growth. In July he didn't reply to Karthik, his roommate from first year, for eleven days. Karthik had asked one question: "Why do you need permission to visit your parents?" When they finally met at the chai stall near Ameerpet, Karthik laid out the months on a napkin: one evening, three evenings, money, the wedding, secrets. Abhinav stared at it. Each step had felt small, even sensible. Seeing them in a row, his chest tightened. "I didn't decide to do all that," he said quietly. "No," Karthik said. "It got decided a little at a time."

qa.q: How many days did Abhinav not reply to Karthik in July?
qa.a: Eleven days.

qa.q: How did Abhinav feel seeing the months written on the napkin?
qa.a: Abhinav felt shaken and uneasy, his chest tightening, as he saw how much had changed when each step had felt small.

qa.q: What made Karthik's approach useful?
qa.a: He laid out the facts in order without insults, letting Abhinav see the whole pattern that is hard to notice from inside.

qa.q: What might Abhinav's family have noticed?
qa.a: They would have seen him miss his cousin's wedding and stop talking about his life, likely leaving them worried and hurt.
